games.explanation: Imanaga's splits are the whole story here, and the market is pretending they don't exist. He's a lefty who handles left-handed bats just fine and gets hit hard by righties, which is inconvenient when Boston's lineup is stacked with the exact profile that has punished him all year, led by a Roman Anthony who's running a .412 xwOBA against right-handers and slides right into the platoon slot. Add a park that plays up on runs but suppresses the homers Imanaga is prone to, and the game script tilts toward a grinding, contact-heavy night rather than the swing-for-the-fences kind he survives. Getting the better team at plus money in that spot is the pitch, and +106 is generous for a coin flip Chicago shouldn't be favored in to begin with.

Houston at home against the Athletics is the kind of line the market prices on reputation, not on who's actually taking the ball. Seth Johnson has been missing bats at a rate that plays against any lineup, and a sim that lands within a run tells you this isn't the mismatch the number implies. Langeliers and Butler give the top of the order enough thump to steal a game that projects as a coin flip, and getting plus money on a coin flip is the entire reason you show up. At +158, the board is paying you to notice that the gap between these teams shrunk the moment the pitching matchup got posted.

Taking the Rays as a dog against Wheeler feels wrong until you remember the price is doing most of the work, and the projected margin is essentially zero. Wheeler is the better arm, nobody's arguing that, but a plus-money line on a game that grades as a coin flip is the entire pitch. Tampa's righty bats up top - Díaz, Caminero, Aranda - are exactly the profile that has scratched runs off elite stuff all year, and Nick Martinez has quietly kept his side in games he had no business being in. At +138 on a projection that lands within a fifth of a run, you're getting paid to be on the wrong name.

Scherzer at 41 is a different pitcher depending on which side of the plate you stand on, and Cincinnati happens to be built to attack the side where he bleeds. The lefty-heavy chunk of this Reds lineup gets to face a Scherzer who's given up a .360 xwOBA to left-handed bats this year, with barrel damage that looks nothing like the guy on the back of the baseball card. Toronto is a small favorite in a game the sim sees as a coin flip, and getting plus money on the coin flip is the entire argument. +150 on a lineup with a real platoon lever to pull is how you get paid for being early.

San Diego is the better team by a real margin, and the market has them as a coin-flip underdog because Randy Vasquez is on the mound and nobody wants to touch that. Fair enough, Vasquez is a walk-and-pray arm, but Arizona's counter is a Diamondbacks lineup that leans heavily on one bat, and Tatis and Machado get to spend the night hunting a starter they're built to punish. A road dog getting plus money with the superior roster and a park that quietly suppresses runs is the kind of shape you take before the number moves. +124 on the better team is the whole argument.

Gilbert is one of the best strikeout arms in the league, and the market has priced this as if that alone decides the game, ignoring that a coin-flip projection at plus money is a gift regardless of who's on the mound. The sim spits out a 3.6 to 3.6 dead heat, which tracks when you remember Kikuchi has been sneaky useful against this Seattle lineup profile and the roof-closed park suppresses the exact kind of damage Gilbert usually surrenders when he does get touched. Trout and Neto are the type of righty bats who can ambush a fastball-heavy arm early, and if the Angels steal two runs in the first three innings, this is suddenly a bullpen game. +155 on a genuine 50/50 is the pitch, and the board is a full seven points behind where it should be.
